query: For single-phase ZrB2 ceramic, which requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and may lack the strength and structural integrity needed for service, what single intervention could lower the required preparation temperature and reduce the holes and eventual component failure caused by prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention and its mechanism, predict its performance compared with conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2, define the relevant preparation and service boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and describe a controlled preparation, integrity, and long-duration exposure experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of single-phase ZrB2 at ~1900 °C under uniaxial pressure will enable >98% theoretical density (reducing residual porosity to <2 vol %) at temperatures ≈400 °C below conventional pressureless sintering, thereby minimizing internal holes and preserving structural integrity during prolonged (∼100 h) exposure to a 900 °C liquid plating bath compared with conventionally prepared ZrB2.
generation.material_initial_state: Cold-pressed ZrB2 powder (1–5 µm) bearing native surface oxides (ZrO2/B2O3 layers) and green-body porosity (~40 %).
generation.intervention: Spark plasma sintering at 1900 °C under 40 MPa uniaxial pressure, 10 min hold time.
generation.conditions: Sintering via SPS at 1800–2000 °C, 30–50 MPa; service exposure in molten plating bath at 800–1000 °C for up to 150 h.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced neck formation and oxide removal by localized plasma, leading to rapid mass transport, pore closure, and network disruption of residual porosity.
generation.mechanism: Pulsed DC current induces Joule heating at particle contacts and transient plasma that cleans surface oxides and accelerates diffusion, enabling densification at lower bulk temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: Achieve >98% theoretical density and <2 vol % open porosity; following 100 h at 900 °C in plating bath, flexural strength retention ≥90% of as-sintered value with minimal new pore formation, versus conventional sinter (92% density, 5 vol % porosity) which loses >50% strength.
generation.baseline: Conventional pressureless sintering at 2300 °C yields ~92% density, ~5 vol % residual porosity, flexural strength ~500 MPa falling to <250 MPa after 100 h in plating bath.
generation.boundary: Valid for ZrB2 powders (1–5 µm), SPS temperature 1800–2000 °C, pressure 30–50 MPa; plating bath 800–1000 °C, exposure ≤150 h.
generation.uncertainty: Moderate – SPS densification of ZrB2 is documented, but long-term molten-salt exposure effects on SPS-processed ZrB2 remain untested.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare two sample sets: (a) ZrB2 by pressureless sintering at 2300 °C, 2 h; (b) ZrB2 by SPS at 1900 °C, 40 MPa, 10 min. Measure density (Archimedes), porosity (micro-CT), pore size distribution, and flexural strength. Subject both to 100 h at 900 °C in a representative molten plating bath. Re-measure the same metrics and perform SEM to assess pore evolution and crack initiation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If SPS-processed ZrB2 does not exceed conventional sintered density by ≥5% or does not retain ≥90% of its initial flexural strength after plating-bath exposure, or shows equivalent pore formation/cracking as the conventionally sintered sample, the hypothesis is falsified.
